ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: <image 1> is the top panel, showing purple/blue-purple stained cell structures on a light-colored background, overall like an ordinary optical microscope or stained section image. <image 2> is the middle panel, showing a light gray-green background and membranous structures inside cells, with pseudo-colored boundaries, similar to an electron microscope or pseudo-colored micrograph. <image 3> is the bottom panel, showing bright multicolored luminous signals on a black background, including fluorescent spots and fluorescent tissue outlines in blue, yellow, purple, orange, etc. Reasoning: The typical characteristic of fluorescence microscope images is bright colored fluorescent signals appearing on a dark background. Among the three candidates, only the bottom panel fits this characteristic. Therefore, the human myocardial image produced by fluorescence microscopy is <image 3>.

raw_record.question_text: Which image label ($<image 1>$, $<image 2>$, or $<image 3>$) shows the human heart muscle produced by fluorescent microscopy?

method.method_draft: First describe the visual appearance of each candidate panel. Then use the rule that fluorescent microscopy is recognized by luminous colored fluorescence signals on a dark background. The only candidate matching this is the bottom panel, which corresponds to <image 3>, so select <image 3>.

planner_metadata.image_role: Inspect the three stacked images: the top panel is a pale stained light-microscope view of rectangular cells, the middle panel is a highly magnified colored ultrastructure-like micrograph, and the bottom panel has a black background with bright multicolored glowing tissue/fiber structures and scattered colored spots. Map the bottom panel to <image 3>.
planner_metadata.text_role: Read the question as asking which of the labeled candidates, <image 1>, <image 2>, or <image 3>, is the human heart muscle image produced by fluorescent microscopy.
planner_metadata.knowledge_role: Fluorescent microscopy typically appears as bright, often multicolored signals against a dark/black background because labeled structures emit light; ordinary light microscopy and electron microscopy do not have this characteristic glowing-on-black appearance.
